paragraphs: The paper studies optimization problems with two nested layers: a smooth vector mapping feeds its output into a smooth outer function. Both layers can involve averages over many components, and the outer function may be nonconvex. This structure makes incremental optimization more complicated because information sampled inside the mapping must also support optimization of the outer function.

The authors extend the SAGA framework to create a composite randomized incremental gradient method. Their analysis measures gradient sample complexity: how much sampled gradient information the method needs. In the general setting, its complexity matches several recently developed approaches based on SVRG. For structured problems admitting linear convergence, however, the proposed method can have a substantial advantage when the problem is ill-conditioned.

A separate result concerns problems where only the inner mapping has a finite-sum structure. Here the method matches SAGA's sample complexity for ordinary smooth nonconvex finite-sum optimization. That result is notable because the outer composition remains present and the sampled composite gradients are biased. The additional structure therefore need not increase the stated sample complexity in this setting.
icml-2019-a-composite-randomized-increme.tldr: A SAGA-based method handles nested finite-sum optimization with competitive sample complexity and potential advantages for structured, ill-conditioned problems.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo permutation tests can support statistical testing when standard parametric assumptions are uncertain or unsuitable. Their computational burden becomes severe when many hypotheses must be tested together: a large simulation budget for each test is multiplied across the entire collection. The paper addresses this scaling problem while retaining the multiple-testing decisions of a full Monte Carlo procedure with high probability.

The proposed Adaptive Monte Carlo Multiple Testing algorithm, AMT, draws on multi-armed bandit theory to allocate simulation effort adaptively. It estimates Monte Carlo p-values and controls the false discovery rate. Its stated sample requirement scales as roughly the number of hypotheses times the square root of the full per-test budget, with logarithmic factors suppressed, rather than their direct product.

The authors prove that this sample complexity is optimal and that AMT agrees with the full procedure with high probability. On a Parkinson genome-wide association dataset, they report reducing runtime from two months to one hour. The result demonstrates that adaptive simulation can make an otherwise costly testing procedure practical while providing a probabilistic agreement guarantee.
icml-2019-adaptive-monte-carlo-multiple-.tldr: AMT adaptively allocates Monte Carlo samples to reproduce full multiple-testing results with high probability at substantially lower computational cost.

paragraphs: This paper considers online optimization in environments that change over time. Performance is measured through adaptive regret, which asks how well a learner performs over every time interval relative to a comparator for that interval. This makes the evaluation sensitive to changing conditions: good performance over the full sequence alone does not establish good performance during each shorter period.

The authors develop adaptive algorithms for loss functions that are both convex and smooth. Earlier work used convexity, while this approach also exploits smoothness to obtain stronger guarantees. The resulting bounds depend on properties of the particular problem and apply over any interval. In particular, they account for how much loss the comparator incurs.

In the worst case, the new regret guarantees remain comparable to existing results. When the comparator achieves a small loss, the bounds become substantially tighter. The benefit is therefore conditional on the difficulty of the interval being evaluated. The work shows how smoothness can support more informative guarantees for changing environments without claiming an improvement of the same size on every sequence.
icml-2019-adaptive-regret-of-convex-and-.tldr: Exploiting smoothness yields adaptive regret bounds that improve when the interval's comparator has low loss while remaining competitive in the worst case.

paragraphs: BayesNAS treats one-shot neural architecture search as compression of an over-parameterized network. The task is to decide which architectural components to retain. The paper highlights two weaknesses in existing approaches: ignoring dependencies between connected nodes can mishandle zero operations, and pruning architecture parameters solely according to their magnitude has a questionable basis.

The proposed method uses hierarchical automatic relevance determination priors to model architecture parameters within a Bayesian framework. This provides a way to address dependencies and assess relevance when selecting the architecture. The authors train the over-parameterized network for one epoch before updating the architecture, making the search procedure computationally economical.

On CIFAR-10, the paper reports completing architecture search for both proxy and proxyless tasks within 0.2 GPU days on a single GPU. It also applies the same approach to convolutional network compression by encouraging structural sparsity. In that application, the authors report highly sparse networks without a loss of accuracy. Together, these findings connect architectural selection and network compression through a shared Bayesian treatment of which structures matter.
icml-2019-bayesnas-a-bayesian-approach-f.tldr: BayesNAS uses Bayesian relevance priors to guide rapid architecture search and structural network compression.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation seeks to transfer a classifier between domains without target-domain labels. Existing theory points toward minimax optimization, which fits naturally with adversarial learning. The paper argues that this broad connection still leaves gaps between theoretical formulations and the scoring functions and margin losses used in practical multiclass classifiers.

The authors extend domain adaptation theory to this multiclass setting and introduce Margin Disparity Discrepancy. This quantity compares distributions in a way tailored to an asymmetric margin loss. They establish generalization bounds for it and design the formulation to fit minimax optimization, making the theoretical comparison directly useful for constructing a training algorithm.

The resulting theory leads to an adversarial domain adaptation method. This matters because the distribution comparison, predictive loss, and optimization procedure are developed together, giving the algorithm a clearer theoretical foundation. Empirical studies report state-of-the-art accuracy on challenging adaptation tasks. Those experiments support the practical value of the approach, while the generalization analysis supplies the formal connection between domain discrepancy and predictive performance.
icml-2019-bridging-theory-and-algorithm-.tldr: Margin Disparity Discrepancy connects multiclass domain adaptation bounds to a practical adversarial training algorithm.

paragraphs: Generalized zero-shot learning requires recognizing classes that were seen during training alongside classes that were not. A central difficulty is bias toward the seen classes: examples from unseen classes can be assigned to familiar categories too readily. The paper addresses this problem by changing the visual representation on which classification operates.

The proposed co-representation network learns a more uniform embedding space. It combines a cooperation module that builds representations with a relation module that performs classification, and the whole network can be trained end to end. The authors also analyze the learned projection mathematically. They find that it has high local linearity and prove a connection between this property and reduced bias.

The representation design therefore has both an architectural motivation and a mathematical explanation for why it can help unseen classes. Experiments report better performance than existing generalized zero-shot methods on several benchmark datasets. The findings support the idea that improving the geometry of the embedding space can reduce the tendency to classify unfamiliar categories as familiar ones, rather than addressing classification only at the final decision stage.
icml-2019-co-representation-network-for-.tldr: A co-representation network learns a more uniform visual embedding to reduce bias toward seen classes in generalized zero-shot learning.

paragraphs: An incomplete multinomial observation identifies a subset of possible categories rather than one definite category. Estimating a model from such observations requires accounting for that ambiguity. The paper develops a maximum likelihood estimation framework for this setting and shows how it also provides a common treatment of several ranking models.

The proposed estimator uses fixed-point iterations through a minorization–maximization type of algorithm. Its update equations involve basic matrix operations, giving the procedure a simple implementation suitable for large datasets. Within the same framework, familiar ranking models such as Bradley–Terry and Plackett–Luce, along with their variants, appear as special cases.

This unification matters because computational improvements to the general estimator can apply across multiple ranking formulations. The authors report that the algorithm needs relatively fewer iterations and less time to converge, and experiments on synthetic and real data show faster execution than existing methods. The contribution combines a shared statistical formulation with an efficient iterative solution, connecting ambiguous categorical observations to practical ranking-data analysis.
icml-2019-fast-and-stable-maximum-likeli.tldr: A simple fixed-point algorithm accelerates maximum likelihood estimation for incomplete multinomial models and several ranking models.

paragraphs: Non-negative matrix factorization learns representations by decomposing data into non-negative factors. Adding orthogonality can make the decomposition more local, which is useful for clustering. Enforcing both requirements simultaneously is difficult, however, and the paper identifies approximate satisfaction of these constraints as a weakness of existing algorithms.

The Greedy Orthogonal Pivoting Algorithm, GOPA, exploits the sparsity of solutions that are both non-negative and orthogonal. It turns the global optimization into a sequence of local problems. At each step, it adaptively selects a subset of coordinates and updates them greedily using closed-form expressions. This structure promotes exact orthogonality while making individual updates manageable.

The authors provide empirical evidence that stronger orthogonality contributes to improved clustering performance. They also develop randomized and parallel versions that can reduce computational cost and improve accuracy, extending the method's usefulness to large datasets. The significance is the link between the solution's structural constraints and an efficient update strategy: sparsity becomes a practical organizing principle for optimization, rather than simply a property checked after fitting.
icml-2019-greedy-orthogonal-pivoting-alg.tldr: GOPA exploits sparse non-negative orthogonal structure to perform local updates, with empirical benefits for clustering and computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Graph sparsification reduces the computational burden of learning on graphs by providing a smaller graph representation. When the graph changes over time, repeatedly rebuilding that representation can itself become expensive. The paper focuses on this maintenance problem, where previous repeated sparsification requires computational work of polynomial order for each update.

The authors introduce fault-tolerant sparsification to reduce that update cost to a constant. The resulting sparse graphs can also make subsequent learning computations substantially cheaper while limiting accuracy loss. The paper gives theoretical upper bounds on the accuracy degradation caused by sparsification for Laplacian-regularized estimation and graph semi-supervised learning.

The framework extends from spectral sparsification to cut sparsification, making it relevant to learning methods based on graph cuts as well. Extensive experiments support the claimed computational efficiency and accuracy on changing graphs. The contribution therefore addresses both sides of using a compact graph representation: keeping it inexpensive to maintain as the graph evolves, and controlling how much its simplification affects the learning task performed afterward.
icml-2019-improved-dynamic-graph-learnin.tldr: Fault-tolerant sparsification reduces graph-update costs to a constant while bounding accuracy loss for subsequent graph learning.

paragraphs: Quantization can make neural networks faster and more energy efficient, but converting a trained floating-point network presents a difficulty. Most weights and activations cluster near the center of their distributions, while a few outliers extend much farther. A linear quantization grid must accommodate this uneven distribution, making the outliers consequential for the conversion.

The paper proposes outlier channel splitting, or OCS. It duplicates channels containing outliers and halves the corresponding channel values. This transformation preserves the network's function while moving the affected values closer to the center of the distribution. It requires no additional training and can be used on commodity hardware.

The approach changes the representation of large values before quantization, avoiding the need to learn a new network solely to manage them. Evaluation on ImageNet classification and language modeling shows that OCS can outperform state-of-the-art clipping methods with only minor overhead. The functional preservation describes the channel transformation itself; the experimental results establish its value for the subsequent quantized model in the evaluated tasks.
icml-2019-improving-neural-network-quant.tldr: Outlier channel splitting preserves a network's function while reducing extreme values, enabling better quantization without retraining.

paragraphs: Randomized sketching provides compact approximations that can make kernel learning more manageable. Applying it online creates an additional challenge: the sketch must be maintained as observations arrive, and that maintenance needs learning guarantees. The paper develops an incremental approach designed around these requirements instead of relying on an offline sketch.

The method constructs two randomized sketches, using a sparse transform matrix and a sampling matrix to approximate the kernel matrix. Rank-one modifications update these sketches incrementally. They then support an explicit feature mapping that changes over time, giving the online learner a representation derived from the evolving approximation.

The analysis establishes an unbiased matrix-product approximation, a kernel-matrix relative-error bound of 1 plus epsilon, and sublinear regret for online learning. It also gives constant time and space costs per round specifically for incremental maintenance. Experiments report better accuracy and efficiency, including in adversarial environments. Together, these results connect approximation quality, online predictive performance, and maintenance cost, showing why an incrementally updateable sketch can be useful beyond its ability to compress a matrix.
icml-2019-incremental-randomized-sketchi.tldr: Incrementally maintained randomized sketches support online kernel learning with approximation guarantees, sublinear regret, and constant per-round maintenance costs.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how adversarial training changes the visual features convolutional networks use to recognize objects. Its central finding is that adversarially trained networks show less of the texture bias found in normally trained networks and develop representations that rely more on shape. The authors study this shift using both visual interpretation and quantitative testing.

First, they compare salience maps on clean images and on images subjected to different transformations. These comparisons reveal that the two kinds of networks can be sensitive to very different features. Second, they construct test datasets that disrupt texture or shape, including style-transferred images, saturated images, and images with shuffled patches.

Classification accuracy on these altered datasets provides quantitative evidence alongside the salience-map comparisons. The combined approach matters because visual explanations alone are complemented by tests of recognition when particular visual information is disrupted. The findings offer insight into why adversarially trained networks are more robust in the studied setting, connecting that robustness to a change in learned representation rather than treating it solely as a prediction-level outcome.
icml-2019-interpreting-adversarially-tra.tldr: Visual and quantitative tests suggest that adversarial training shifts CNN object recognition away from texture and toward shape.

paragraphs: A task reward can identify successful behavior without encouraging multiple distinct ways to succeed. This paper develops a reinforcement learning method that seeks a collection of policies for the same task. Each policy should earn task reward while producing behavior that differs from policies already discovered.

The method adds a novelty reward based on sequences of visited states. Autoencoders trained on sequences from previous policies provide the basis for measuring how novel another sequence is. A two-objective policy-gradient update then balances improvement in task reward against improvement in novelty reward. This makes diversity part of the learning process while retaining the original task objective.

The authors demonstrate collections of task-solving policies with distinct action sequences on maze navigation, a simulated robot-arm reaching task, and hopper locomotion. They also report effectiveness on deceptive tasks where policy-gradient methods often become stuck. These findings show the practical value of evaluating behavior relative to previously learned policies: the learner can pursue alternative solutions while continuing to account for whether those solutions accomplish the task.
icml-2019-learning-novel-policies-for-ta.tldr: A policy-gradient method balances task reward with autoencoder-based novelty to learn multiple distinct policies that solve the same task.

paragraphs: In a generative adversarial network, the discriminator must provide a useful gradient to guide the generator. The paper shows that unrestricted discriminator function spaces commonly produce gradients that fail to provide this guidance. It contrasts this with Wasserstein GANs, whose 1-Lipschitz restriction avoids the identified gradient problem.

The authors also examine a compact dual formulation of Wasserstein distance with a relaxed Lipschitz condition. They show that this relaxation can theoretically reintroduce uninformative gradients. Motivated by that distinction, they study a general formulation with Lipschitz constraints and introduce a family called Lipschitz GANs, or LGANs.

For LGANs, the paper establishes existence and uniqueness of the optimal discriminator and a unique Nash equilibrium. It also proves that the family is generally capable of eliminating the gradient uninformativeness problem. Empirical analysis reports greater stability and consistently higher sample quality than WGAN. The work therefore connects a restriction on the discriminator to both formal properties of the learning game and observed training behavior, while distinguishing theoretical guarantees from experimental comparisons.
icml-2019-lipschitz-generative-adversari.tldr: Lipschitz GANs constrain discriminators to address uninformative generator gradients, with theoretical guarantees and empirical improvements over WGAN.

paragraphs: The paper asks how much computation is fundamentally required to optimize an average of smooth, nonconvex component functions. Earlier lower bounds largely concerned convex components, leaving less clarity about the limits of algorithms in the nonconvex setting. A lower bound establishes a benchmark for judging whether an algorithm's complexity can be improved.

The authors prove tight complexity lower bounds for finding approximately optimal points and approximately stationary points in different settings. Their analysis covers a broad range of curvature conditions expressed through the smallest Hessian eigenvalue of the objective or its individual components. These settings matter because the allowable curvature helps determine the difficulty of the optimization problem.

The results show that KatyushaX, Natasha, and StagewiseKatyusha attain optimal incremental first-order oracle complexity up to logarithmic factors in the corresponding settings. This concerns the number of oracle calls, rather than a blanket claim about every aspect of runtime. The paper also identifies possible routes to stronger complexity results through additional assumptions or different convergence analyses, clarifying both established limits and opportunities for further progress.
icml-2019-lower-bounds-for-smooth-noncon.tldr: Tight lower bounds show that several nonconvex finite-sum algorithms already achieve optimal oracle complexity up to logarithmic factors in the studied settings.

paragraphs: In multi-goal reinforcement learning, one policy learns behavior conditioned on different goals. Training often reuses trajectories drawn randomly from a replay buffer. The paper points out that the goals achieved in this buffer reflect the behavior policies that collected them, so random replay can preserve an uneven distribution of experience.

When no prior information about the target goal distribution is available, the authors motivate learning uniformly from diverse achieved goals through a Bayesian perspective. They introduce a weighted-entropy objective that encourages both high expected return and greater goal diversity. A maximum-entropy prioritization framework then supports optimization of this combined objective.

The framework is evaluated with Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient, both with and without Hindsight Experience Replay, on multi-goal robotic tasks from OpenAI Gym. The experiments report promising improvements in performance and sample efficiency relative to the tested baselines. The contribution links the distribution of replayed experience to what the agent is encouraged to learn, making diversity among achieved goals an explicit consideration in the training objective.
icml-2019-maximum-entropy-regularized-mu.tldr: A weighted-entropy objective and replay prioritization framework encourage diverse achieved goals, with promising gains on multi-goal robotic tasks.

paragraphs: The metric used to judge a deployed model can be more complicated than the loss used to train it. Training and test data may also follow different distributions. This paper addresses these issues by learning how much weight to place on individual training examples, using validation performance to guide those choices.

The model is trained with a standard loss multiplied by learned example weights. Those weights are optimized for the desired test metric on a validation set. The approach builds on connections between complex evaluation metrics and cost-weighted learning, allowing the evaluation objective to influence training through the importance assigned to examples.

The authors state that the weights can be learned for any test metric, including black-box metrics and application-specific measures. They illustrate the method on public benchmarks and real applications and provide a generalization bound. The contribution is a flexible interface between an ordinary training loss and a potentially complicated evaluation criterion. It places the adaptation in the example weights, so the chosen metric can shape learning without requiring the standard loss itself to become that metric.
icml-2019-metric-optimized-example-weigh.tldr: Learning training-example weights against a validation metric lets standard losses target complex or black-box evaluation objectives.

paragraphs: A common strategy for unsupervised domain adaptation learns features that look similar across domains while maintaining low classification error on the source. This paper shows that those two properties are insufficient to guarantee success on the target. Its counterexample involves conditional shift, where feature distributions within classes differ between source and target.

The authors develop a generalization upper bound that explicitly accounts for this shift and provides a sufficient condition for adaptation. This changes what must be considered when evaluating a representation: similarity between the overall domain distributions and source accuracy alone can overlook differences in how features relate to classes.

The paper also proves an information-theoretic lower bound on joint source and target error for methods learning invariant representations. When the marginal label distributions differ, the result identifies a fundamental tradeoff between invariance and low error across both domains. Experiments on real datasets corroborate the theoretical findings. The message is conditional but consequential: distribution alignment needs to be understood together with class relationships and label proportions when designing adaptation methods.
icml-2019-on-learning-invariant-represen.tldr: Domain-invariant features and low source error do not guarantee adaptation, with conditional shift and differing label proportions creating important obstacles.

paragraphs: This paper studies privacy amplification through subsampling within Rényi differential privacy. The issue is central to moments-accountant methods used in differentially private deep learning: privacy analysis must track what happens when a mechanism operates on a sampled portion of the data. The sampling rule is therefore part of the mathematical problem.

The authors analyze Poisson subsampling, where each data point is selected independently by a coin toss. This differs from earlier treatments based on sampling with replacement. For this independent-selection scheme, they derive simpler and tighter bounds on the privacy of subsampled mechanisms and develop approximation methods designed to remain numerically stable.

For subsampled Gaussian and Laplace mechanisms, the paper proves analytical Rényi privacy formulas that match the lower bound exactly. This establishes tightness for those mechanisms in the studied setting. Numerical results demonstrate an order-of-magnitude improvement in the privacy–utility tradeoff. The contribution combines sharper privacy accounting with practical numerical evaluation, showing how a precise treatment of the sampling scheme can materially improve the resulting privacy analysis.
icml-2019-poission-subsampled-renyi-diff.tldr: Analyzing Poisson subsampling yields tighter Rényi privacy bounds, stable approximations, and exact formulas for subsampled Gaussian and Laplace mechanisms.

paragraphs: Many models describe a high-dimensional observation through shared hidden features and a separate vector of feature strengths for each object. Each non-negative entry indicates how strongly one feature contributes to that object. This paper focuses on modeling correlations among those strengths, allowing the use of one hidden feature to be statistically related to the use of others.

The authors introduce population random measure embedding, or PRME, which places random-function priors on the feature-loading vectors. They interpret the construction as a generalization of a paintbox model using random functions. Its Bayesian nonparametric foundation comes from applying a representation theorem for separately exchangeable discrete random measures.

To learn the model efficiently, the paper uses neural networks within amortized variational inference. The contribution thus joins a probabilistic construction for correlated feature loadings with a computational approach for fitting it. The correlations live in the strengths assigned to shared features, which directly determine how those features participate in explaining each observation. This gives the dependence model a clear role within the larger likelihood formulation.
icml-2019-random-function-priors-for-cor.tldr: PRME uses random-function priors to model correlated feature strengths and neural amortized inference to learn the resulting Bayesian nonparametric model.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning can use data efficiently, but image observations make it difficult to construct a useful model for control. SOLAR addresses this by learning representations suited to repeated model-based policy improvement, including when the underlying system has complex dynamics. The representation is shaped by what the control procedure needs to infer.

Specifically, the learned representation supports simple dynamics and cost models fitted from data collected by the current policy. This allows a method based on the linear-quadratic regulator to operate on systems observed through images. The key connection is between representation learning and control: the representation is optimized to make the models used for policy improvement tractable.

The authors evaluate the approach on several robotics tasks, including manipulation by a real robotic arm controlled directly from images. They report substantially better final performance than other model-based methods and significantly greater efficiency than model-free reinforcement learning. These findings support the usefulness of learning a representation around the requirements of iterative control, even when the raw observations and physical dynamics are complicated.
icml-2019-solar-deep-structured-represen.tldr: SOLAR learns image representations that support simple control models, enabling efficient model-based learning on robotic tasks.

paragraphs: Sparse models restrict which variables can participate in a solution, but some applications require those variables to follow a graph structure. Such constraints can be nonconvex and more complicated than standard sparsity norms capture. The paper targets this setting, which arises in applications including disease outbreaks and social networks.

The authors propose a stochastic gradient-based algorithm for optimization under graph-structured sparsity constraints. Stochastic updates offer inexpensive individual iterations, making them attractive for large datasets. The method is not restricted to least-squares loss, extending its scope beyond that particular objective while retaining the graph-based constraint.

The theoretical result is linear convergence up to a constant error. This means the guarantee describes rapid progress toward an error level, rather than exact convergence with no residual error. The authors describe the guarantee as competitive with batch-learning counterparts and report extensive experiments supporting efficiency and effectiveness. The contribution brings inexpensive stochastic optimization to a structured sparsity setting where conventional norm-based treatments cannot be applied directly, while supplying a qualified convergence guarantee.
icml-2019-stochastic-iterative-hard-thre.tldr: A stochastic method handles nonconvex graph-structured sparsity beyond least squares, with linear convergence up to a constant error.

paragraphs: This paper develops a theoretical account of the tradeoff between ordinary classification accuracy and resistance to adversarial examples. It separates robust prediction error into natural classification error and boundary error. This decomposition makes the relationship between the two objectives explicit and provides a basis for designing a defense.

Using classification-calibrated loss theory, the authors derive a differentiable upper bound on robust error. They show that it is the tightest bound of its kind uniformly over all probability distributions and measurable predictors. That uniform tightness is a property of the theoretical bound, giving the subsequent algorithm a principled target for balancing accuracy and robustness.

The resulting defense, TRADES, turns this analysis into a method for trading adversarial robustness against accuracy. The paper reports strong experimental performance on real datasets. Its methodology also underpinned the authors' winning entry in the stated adversarial vision challenge, exceeding the runner-up by 11.41% in mean L2 perturbation distance. The contribution connects an error decomposition, a sharp bound, and an empirically effective training method.
icml-2019-theoretically-principled-trade.tldr: TRADES uses a tight theoretical bound on robust error to guide the balance between adversarial robustness and classification accuracy.

paragraphs: Noise has been empirically associated with effective neural-network training, but explaining its role mathematically is harder. This paper studies that question in a simple two-layer convolutional network. Its optimization problem is nonconvex and contains both a spurious local optimum and a global optimum, providing a setting where becoming trapped is a concrete concern.

The authors analyze perturbed gradient descent combined with noise annealing. For the studied model, they prove convergence to a global optimum in polynomial time from arbitrary initialization. The result shows that the added noise enables the algorithm to escape the spurious local optimum efficiently rather than remaining trapped there.

Numerical experiments support the theoretical analysis. The significance is a rigorous example of noise actively helping optimization navigate a problematic landscape. The guarantee applies to the particular simple network studied and to the combination of perturbations with annealing. Within that setting, it connects the use of noise to both successful escape from a misleading optimum and an efficient route to a global solution.
icml-2019-toward-understanding-the-impor.tldr: For a simple two-layer CNN, perturbed gradient descent with noise annealing provably reaches a global optimum in polynomial time from arbitrary initialization.

paragraphs: The paper studies whether poisoned training images can induce a targeted error in a convolutional network whose outputs, architecture, and parameters are unavailable to the attacker. The desired outcome is specific: after training on the contaminated data, the unknown model assigns a chosen target image to a particular class.

The attack constructs several slightly perturbed images from a base class. In feature space, these images are arranged so that their convex polytope contains the target image. This geometric objective is intended to make the target associated with the poison images' class after training, while operating in the clean-label poisoning setting.

The authors find that using Dropout during poison construction and applying the objective at multiple layers improves transferability. They demonstrate attacks in both transfer-learning and end-to-end training settings, reporting transferable success rates above 50% while poisoning 1% of the training set. These are demonstrated outcomes rather than a guarantee for every unknown model. The findings show that limited knowledge of the eventual network does not, by itself, prevent targeted training-data poisoning from transferring.
icml-2019-transferable-clean-label-poiso.tldr: Feature-space poison construction transfers targeted clean-label attacks to unknown networks, with reported success above 50% at 1% training-set poisoning.
